label: copy-phase input of the letter l
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase, at steps whose input is the letter l (the model fed back the l it just output). Never fires in the original phase (including on l inputs there), at the delimiter, or on any other input token. Recall is 100% on dev; about 17% of copy-phase l inputs stay inactive. Firing rate and magnitude go up later in the copy phase: the rate climbs from ~0.4% at t=5 to ~3% at t>=12, and the top activations come from l tokens late in long sequences. Restricting to the last few steps lowers F1, so the simple predicate is kept.

issues: Factual claims check out. On dev, all 75,867 active steps are in the copy phase with in_tok = l. Activation is 0 in the original phase, 0 at the delimiter, and 0 on every other input token. On test the predicate scores precision 0.828, recall 1.0, F1 0.906, mass recall 1.0, and coverage is 1.0 in every activation quartile.

No missed activations on test (0 steps). The 15,663 false positives (copy-phase l inputs that stay inactive) do not form a clean class. Splitting them by recall_idx, L, in_count / repeated l, prev_tok type, next_out, out_tok type, n_digits, to_go and correct only changes precision gradually, within about 0.65 to 0.92 (lowest at recall_idx==1 with 0.65; highest with prev_tok a digit or at to_go==0, 0.92). This looks like a magnitude threshold on a continuous signal, not a separate counterexample class.
Refinements did not beat the base predicate on test F1: recall_idx>=2 gave 0.862, excluding (recall_idx==1 & L>=6) gave 0.875, and excluding (recall_idx<=2 & L>=7) gave 0.846, all below 0.906.

Minor wording point: the '0.4% at t=5 to 3% at t>=12' figures are the overall per-step firing rate. Most of that rise comes from more of the steps at later t being copy-phase steps, not only from l inputs becoming more likely to fire. The trend is still real: precision rises from 0.65 at recall_idx==1 to about 0.87 at recall_idx>=2.
